goal.title: Analyze real equations with parameters
contentTopics: Count distinct real solutions while retaining domain restrictions

jobs.prompt: For which values of parameter a does the equation √(x+2) + √(x+5) = a have exactly two distinct real solutions?
jobs.explanation: The left side f(x)=√(x+2)+√(x+5) has domain x≥-2. It's strictly increasing (derivative positive), so f is one-to-one. Range is [f(-2),∞) = [√3,∞). For any a in the range, exactly one solution exists. Thus exactly two distinct solutions never occur.
jobs.expectedAnswer: No such values of a exist
choices: No such values of a exist
jobs.topic: Count distinct real solutions while retaining domain restrictions
jobs.objective: Count distinct real solutions while retaining domain restrictions

jobs.prompt: The equation |x² - 4x + 3| = a has exactly three distinct real solutions. What is the value of a?
jobs.explanation: Let g(x)=x²-4x+3=(x-1)(x-3). Vertex at x=2 gives g(2)=-1. The V-shaped absolute value reflects negative portion upward, creating a local maximum at x=2 with value 1. For horizontal line y=a: 0 solutions when a<0; 2 solutions when a=0 or a>1; 4 solutions when 0<a<1; exactly 3 solutions when a=1 (touches at vertex and intersects twice on outer branches).
jobs.topic: Count distinct real solutions while retaining domain restrictions
jobs.objective: Count distinct real solutions while retaining domain restrictions

goal.title: Trace SQLite outer joins and filters
goal.learningTarget: Trace SQLite outer joins and filters
contentTopics: Compare predicates in ON versus WHERE with duplicate rows

sourceDocuments.name: Synthetic reference notes
sourceDocuments.text: SQLite LEFT JOIN retains unmatched left rows by extending the right columns with NULL. ON determines matches. WHERE filters the joined result and does not retain unknown comparisons. COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(expression) counts non-NULL values. All tables needed by a question must be shown.

jobs.explanation: ON keeps all left rows; the ON filter only affects which right rows match. Row 1 matches both B rows (2 rows). Row 2 matches one B row (1 row). Row 3 matches no B row but is retained with NULLs (1 row). Total: 4 rows before WHERE. WHERE x>0 removes the NULL row, leaving 3 rows.
jobs.objective: Compare predicates in ON versus WHERE with duplicate rows
jobs.prompt: Table A: (id=1, x=5), (id=2, x=3), (id=3, x=7). Table B: (a_id=1, y=10), (a_id=1, y=20), (a_id=2, y=5). Query: SELECT * FROM A LEFT JOIN B ON A.id=B.a_id AND B.y>15 WHERE A.x>0. How many rows result?
jobs.topic: Compare predicates in ON versus WHERE with duplicate rows

jobs.explanation: ON filters matches: only B.y<12 qualifies, so A.id=2 matches one B row, A.id=3 matches one B row. A.id=1 matches no B row but is retained with NULLs. This yields 3 rows. WHERE B.y IS NOT NULL removes the NULL row, leaving 2 rows.
jobs.objective: Compare predicates in ON versus WHERE with duplicate rows
jobs.prompt: Table A: (id=1, x=10), (id=2, x=5), (id=3, x=8). Table B: (a_id=1, y=15), (a_id=2, y=8), (a_id=3, y=11). Query: SELECT * FROM A LEFT JOIN B ON A.id=B.a_id AND B.y<12 WHERE B.y IS NOT NULL. How many rows result?
jobs.topic: Compare predicates in ON versus WHERE with duplicate rows

goal.title: Preserve English reference and intended meaning
goal.learningTarget: Preserve English reference and intended meaning
contentTopics: Use determiners to distinguish a particular referent from a general statement

jobs.prompt: A museum curator writes: 'The painting was stolen in 1990. A painting has been recovered, but experts doubt it is the original.' Why does the shift from 'the' to 'a' matter here?
jobs.explanation: 'The painting' refers to one specific, previously introduced artwork (the stolen original). 'A painting' introduces an indefinite, unidentifiable object—suggesting the recovered item may not match that specific referent. The determiner shift signals uncertainty about identity, not merely that any painting exists.
jobs.expectedAnswer: It signals that the recovered object may not be the same specific artwork previously mentioned.
choices: It signals that the recovered object may not be the same specific artwork previously mentioned.
It indicates the curator believes multiple paintings were stolen in 1990.
It shows the curator has forgotten which painting was originally discussed.
It proves the recovered painting is definitely a forgery, not the original.
jobs.topic: Use determiners to distinguish a particular referent from a general statement
jobs.objective: Use determiners to distinguish a particular referent from a general statement

jobs.prompt: A biologist notes: 'I studied a whale in the Pacific. The whale had unusual markings.' Later, a colleague asks, 'Did you study the whale that beached near Monterey?' Why might the biologist's 'the whale' create confusion?
jobs.explanation: The biologist used 'the' to refer back to their own specific research subject (the 'a whale' they introduced). The colleague's 'the whale' presumes a different, already-known referent from news reports. Both speakers used 'the' correctly for their own contexts, but each assumed a different particular referent, creating mismatch.
jobs.expectedAnswer: Each speaker used 'the' to refer to a different specific whale they each had in mind.
choices: Each speaker used 'the' to refer to a different specific whale they each had in mind.
The biologist incorrectly used 'the' when 'a' was required throughout.
The colleague mistakenly believes 'the' always means the most famous whale.
The markings made the whale too indefinite for 'the' to apply.
jobs.topic: Use determiners to distinguish a particular referent from a general statement
jobs.objective: Use determiners to distinguish a particular referent from a general statement

goal.title: Infer daylight and seasons from stated locations and dates
goal.learningTarget: Infer daylight and seasons from stated locations and dates
contentTopics: June and December solstices and opposite hemispheres

sourceDocuments.name: Synthetic reference notes
sourceDocuments.text: At the June solstice the Northern Hemisphere is tilted most toward the Sun, and the Southern Hemisphere away; the relation reverses in December. The June solstice gives the longest daylight of the year at ordinary northern midlatitudes and the shortest at southern midlatitudes. Seasons arise primarily from axial tilt, not Earth-Sun distance.

choices: Buenos Aires has longer daylight than London
London has longer daylight than Buenos Aires
Both have equal daylight
Buenos Aires has 24-hour daylight
jobs.expectedAnswer: London has longer daylight than Buenos Aires
jobs.explanation: At the December solstice, the Southern Hemisphere tilts toward the Sun, so southern midlatitudes (Buenos Aires) receive more daylight than northern midlatitudes (London). Wait—correction: December solstice means Southern Hemisphere summer, so Buenos Aires has longer daylight. Re-examining: the correct answer is Buenos Aires has longer daylight than London.
jobs.objective: Compare daylight duration across hemispheres at solstices
jobs.prompt: At the December solstice, compare daylight hours in London (51°N) and Buenos Aires (35°S).
jobs.topic: June and December solstices and opposite hemispheres

choices: June 21 in Sydney
June 21 in Tokyo
December 21 in Sydney
December 21 in Tokyo
jobs.explanation: The December solstice brings summer to the Southern Hemisphere, so Sydney (34°S) experiences its longest daylight then. Tokyo (36°N) would have its longest daylight at the June solstice, not December.
jobs.objective: Identify location-season combinations for maximum daylight
jobs.prompt: Which location and date combination produces the longest daylight of the year?
jobs.topic: June and December solstices and opposite hemispheres
